Question 1: Compare KNN and logistic regression

Use breast-cancer.csv, which contains 569 cases from the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer dataset. Predict y (1 for malignant and 0 for benign) using mean_radius, mean_texture, and mean_smoothness.

Set a random seed and randomly split the observations into 70% training and 30% test data. Use the same split for every model. Standardize the predictors using the training means and standard deviations, and apply the same transformations to the test data.

Fit ordinary logistic regression with an intercept and no penalty, and KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{5,15,25,35,45}. k\in\{5,15,25,35,45\}.

Using the estimated probabilities for y = 1 on the test data, plot all six ROC curves in one figure and report their AUC values. Which of the six fitted models do you prefer? Give a brief justification based on your results.

Answer

I wrote the KNN classifier myself so that the estimated probability of y = 1 is the fraction of the kk nearest training observations that are malignant. The same distance matrix is reused for every kk.

bc <- read.csv("data/breast-cancer.csv")
predictors <- c("mean_radius", "mean_texture", "mean_smoothness")

set.seed(43206)
n <- nrow(bc)
train_id <- sample(n, round(0.7 * n))          # 70% training, 30% test
train <- bc[train_id, ]
test  <- bc[-train_id, ]
c(n_train = nrow(train), n_test = nrow(test), malignant_rate = mean(train$y))
       n_train         n_test malignant_rate 
    398.000000     171.000000       0.361809 
# standardize with TRAINING means and standard deviations, applied to both sets
center <- colMeans(train[, predictors])
scale_ <- apply(train[, predictors], 2, sd)
Z_train <- scale(train[, predictors], center = center, scale = scale_)
Z_test  <- scale(test[, predictors],  center = center, scale = scale_)

# ROC curve and AUC from estimated probabilities (AUC via the Mann-Whitney identity)
roc_curve <- function(prob, y) {
  o <- order(prob, decreasing = TRUE); y <- y[o]
  list(fpr = c(0, cumsum(y == 0) / sum(y == 0)),
       tpr = c(0, cumsum(y == 1) / sum(y == 1)))
}
auc_value <- function(prob, y) {
  r <- rank(prob); n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

# KNN probability that y = 1: the fraction of the k nearest neighbours that are malignant
knn_prob <- function(D, y_train, k) apply(D, 1, function(d) mean(y_train[order(d)[1:k]]))

# rows = test observations, columns = training observations
D_test <- as.matrix(dist(rbind(Z_train, Z_test)))[nrow(Z_train) + seq_len(nrow(Z_test)),
                                                  seq_len(nrow(Z_train))]
logit_fit <- glm(y ~ ., data = data.frame(Z_train, y = train$y), family = binomial)
p_logit   <- predict(logit_fit, newdata = data.frame(Z_test), type = "response")

ks <- c(5, 15, 25, 35, 45)
p_knn <- sapply(ks, function(k) knn_prob(D_test, train$y, k))
colnames(p_knn) <- paste0("k=", ks)

auc_all <- c(Logistic = auc_value(p_logit, test$y),
             apply(p_knn, 2, auc_value, y = test$y))
round(auc_all, 4)
Logistic      k=5     k=15     k=25     k=35     k=45 
  0.9759   0.9438   0.9621   0.9697   0.9757   0.9764 
cols <- c("black", "firebrick", "darkorange", "darkgreen", "steelblue", "purple")
plot(0:1, 0:1, type = "n", xlab = "False positive rate", ylab = "True positive rate",
     main = "Test ROC curves: logistic regression and KNN", asp = 1)
abline(0, 1, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
r <- roc_curve(p_logit, test$y)
lines(r$fpr, r$tpr, col = cols[1], lwd = 2)
for (j in seq_along(ks)) {
  r <- roc_curve(p_knn[, j], test$y)
  lines(r$fpr, r$tpr, col = cols[j + 1], lwd = 1.6)
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = cols, cex = 0.85,
       legend = sprintf("%-10s AUC %.4f", names(auc_all), auc_all))

Which model I prefer. Logistic regression, with AUC 0.97590.9759. Two reasons from these results.

First, it is at least as accurate as every KNN fit. Among the KNN models, AUC increases steadily with kk, from 0.94380.9438 at k=5k=5 to 0.97640.9764 at k=45k=45, and only the largest neighbourhoods come close to the logistic fit. Small kk clearly overfits: with three predictors and 398 training observations, a five-point neighbourhood gives a noisy probability estimate that takes only the six values 0,0.2,…,10,0.2,\ldots,1.

Second, the KNN curve is still improving at the largest kk tested, so k=45k=45 is not a tuned optimum; it is the edge of the given grid, and a fair comparison would require selecting kk by cross-validation on the training data. Logistic regression reaches comparable accuracy with three slopes and an intercept, gives continuous probability estimates rather than multiples of 1/k1/k, and is directly interpretable through its coefficients. With this sample size and these three predictors, the extra flexibility of KNN buys nothing.

The difference is small in absolute terms, and a single test split of 171 observations cannot resolve AUC differences of a few thousandths. I prefer logistic regression on the combination of equal-or-better accuracy and greater simplicity, not on the strength of the AUC gap alone.

Question 2: Training and test ROC curves

Use the same data, training/test split, and standardization as in Question 1. Fit KNN with Euclidean distance, equal neighbor weights, and

k∈{1,3,5,10,20}. k\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

Use each fitted model to estimate probabilities for both the training and test observations. For training predictions, include each observation itself among its kk nearest neighbors.

For each kk, use a separate panel to show the training and test ROC curves together. Report both AUC values.

Explain the difference between training and test performance and how it changes with kk. In particular, explain what happens at k=1k=1 and why training performance may not reflect performance on new observations.

Answer

ks2 <- c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20)

# training predictions: each observation is its own first neighbour (distance 0)
D_train <- as.matrix(dist(Z_train))

p_tr <- sapply(ks2, function(k) knn_prob(D_train, train$y, k))
p_te <- sapply(ks2, function(k) knn_prob(D_test,  train$y, k))
colnames(p_tr) <- colnames(p_te) <- paste0("k=", ks2)

auc_tab <- data.frame(
  k        = ks2,
  train_AUC = apply(p_tr, 2, auc_value, y = train$y),
  test_AUC  = apply(p_te, 2, auc_value, y = test$y))
auc_tab$gap <- auc_tab$train_AUC - auc_tab$test_AUC
round(auc_tab, 4)
      k train_AUC test_AUC    gap
k=1   1    1.0000   0.8900 0.1100
k=3   3    0.9893   0.9427 0.0467
k=5   5    0.9863   0.9438 0.0425
k=10 10    0.9844   0.9557 0.0287
k=20 20    0.9826   0.9602 0.0224
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
for (j in seq_along(ks2)) {
  plot(0:1, 0:1, type = "n", xlab = "False positive rate", ylab = "True positive rate",
       main = sprintf("k = %d", ks2[j]), asp = 1)
  abline(0, 1, lty = 3, col = "grey60")
  r <- roc_curve(p_tr[, j], train$y); lines(r$fpr, r$tpr, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
  r <- roc_curve(p_te[, j], test$y);  lines(r$fpr, r$tpr, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
  legend("bottomright", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, lwd = 2,
         col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
         legend = sprintf(c("train %.4f", "test  %.4f"),
                          c(auc_tab$train_AUC[j], auc_tab$test_AUC[j])))
}
plot.new()
legend("center", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
       legend = c("Training ROC", "Test ROC"), title = "Curves")
par(op)

The difference between training and test performance.

Training AUC is higher than test AUC at every kk, and the gap shrinks steadily as kk grows: 0.110 at k=1k=1, down to 0.022 at k=20k=20. The two move in opposite directions. Training AUC falls with kk (from 11 to 0.98260.9826) while test AUC rises (from 0.89000.8900 to 0.96020.9602).

This is the bias-variance trade-off seen through the training/test gap. Small kk means a flexible, low-bias, high-variance rule: each prediction depends on very few observations, so it adapts to the particular noise in the training sample. Large kk averages over a wide neighbourhood, which smooths away that noise (lower variance) at the cost of blurring the boundary between classes (higher bias). The training curve rewards the flexibility that the test curve penalizes, which is why the gap is a direct measure of overfitting rather than of quality.

What happens at k=1k=1.

Training AUC is exactly 11. Because each training observation is included among its own neighbours and sits at distance zero from itself, the single nearest neighbour of a training point is that point. The estimated probability is therefore its own label, 00 or 11, so every malignant case is ranked strictly above every benign case and the ROC curve passes through the top-left corner. The fit reproduces the training labels perfectly.

That perfect score measures memorization, not prediction. On the test data, where self-matching is impossible, the same model has the worst AUC of the five, 0.89000.8900. The training AUC of 11 is not a slightly optimistic estimate of this number; it is uninformative about it.

Why training performance need not reflect performance on new observations.

The training error is evaluated on the same observations that defined the fitted rule, so it is optimistic by construction, and the more flexible the method, the larger that optimism. At k=1k=1 the optimism is total. As kk grows, each prediction averages over kk neighbours and the self-contribution shrinks to a weight of 1/k1/k, so the training estimate becomes less self-referential and the gap narrows to 0.022 at k=20k=20. Even then it does not vanish.

The practical consequence is that kk must never be chosen by training performance: that criterion is monotonically optimized by k=1k=1, the worst model here on new data. Honest selection requires held-out data, through cross-validation on the training set or a separate validation set.

Answer

My peer-grading assignment (issue #1) gave me the Homework 5 reports of mazy2005 and stallur10.

1. The item I selected.

Report: stallur10, Question 2, the final paragraph answering why the nonlinear terms in the response model affect the KNN-versus-lasso comparison.

The report claims that lasso’s linear fit captures nothing but the average level of the two nonlinear terms, and that this disadvantage would persist even if the correct nonlinear terms were added to the model. Both halves of that claim are wrong. A linear term in X2X_2 captures most of the variation in sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2), and adding the correct nonlinear terms removes the disadvantage entirely rather than leaving it in place.

2. My assessment.

The sentence I am responding to is:

“This is a structural disadvantage unrelated to correlation, and would remain even with the correct nonlinear terms.”

This statement could be improved because if the correct nonlinear terms, such as sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, were included as predictors, then the lasso would no longer have the same structural disadvantage of being unable to represent the true response function. A clearer explanation would be that the disadvantage comes from fitting lasso using only the original linear predictors, rather than from lasso itself. The response could distinguish this model-specification issue from the separate effect of correlation on KNN performance.

3. A corrected answer.

Here is how I would rewrite stallur10’s final Question 2 paragraph.

Lasso fits a linear combination of the supplied covariates, so with only the 30 raw covariates it cannot reproduce sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) or −0.3X32-0.3X_3^2 exactly. But it is not limited to their average level. The best linear predictor keeps whatever part of each nonlinear term is correlated with a covariate, and discards only the orthogonal remainder.

For X2∼𝒩(0,1)X_2\sim\mathcal N(0,1), the relevant quantities are Cov⁡(X2,sin⁡X2)=E(X2sin⁡X2)=e−1/2≈0.6065,Var⁡(sin⁡X2)=1−e−22≈0.4323.\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,\sin X_2)=E(X_2\sin X_2)=e^{-1/2}\approx0.6065,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\sin X_2)=\tfrac{1-e^{-2}}{2}\approx0.4323 . So the best linear approximation uses slope 0.60650.6065 and explains Cov⁡(X2,sin⁡X2)2Var⁡(X2)Var⁡(sin⁡X2)=e−1(1−e−2)/2≈0.851\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_2,\sin X_2)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X_2)\operatorname{Var}(\sin X_2)}=\frac{e^{-1}}{(1-e^{-2})/2}\approx0.851 of the variance of sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2): about 85%85\%, not zero. Only the remaining 15%15\% is lost.

The quadratic term behaves in the opposite way. Since X3X_3 is symmetric about zero, Cov⁡(X3,X32)=E(X33)=0\operatorname{Cov}(X_3,X_3^2)=E(X_3^3)=0, so no linear term in X3X_3 helps. Here the intercept really does absorb only the mean, E(−0.3X32)=−0.3E(-0.3X_3^2)=-0.3, leaving the full Var⁡(−0.3X32)=0.18\operatorname{Var}(-0.3X_3^2)=0.18 unexplained. The two nonlinear terms are therefore not equivalent, and the blanket statement covering both is wrong.

Adding these up, the approximation error of the best linear rule is about 0.15×0.4323+0.18≈0.2450.15\times0.4323+0.18\approx0.245, which is close to the observed lasso test MSE of 0.3390.339 and 0.2140.214 and far above the noise floor σ2=0.01\sigma^2=0.01. Most of lasso’s error in this simulation is approximation error, not estimation error.

library(glmnet)

cat(sprintf("Cov(X2, sin X2) = %.4f   Var(sin X2) = %.4f   R^2 of linear term = %.4f\n",
            exp(-0.5), (1 - exp(-2)) / 2, exp(-1) / ((1 - exp(-2)) / 2)))
Cov(X2, sin X2) = 0.6065   Var(sin X2) = 0.4323   R^2 of linear term = 0.8509
cat(sprintf("Var(-0.3 X3^2)  = %.4f   captured by a linear term in X3 = %.4f\n", 0.18, 0))
Var(-0.3 X3^2)  = 0.1800   captured by a linear term in X3 = 0.0000
set.seed(20251)
n_tr <- 400; p30 <- 30; n_te <- 1000

simulate <- function(rho) {
  Sigma <- matrix(rho, p30, p30); diag(Sigma) <- 1
  X <- matrix(rnorm((n_tr + n_te) * p30), n_tr + n_te, p30) %*% chol(Sigma)
  y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 + rnorm(n_tr + n_te, 0, 0.1)
  list(X_tr = X[1:n_tr, ], y_tr = y[1:n_tr], X_te = X[-(1:n_tr), ], y_te = y[-(1:n_tr)])
}
augment <- function(X) cbind(X, sin(X[, 2]), X[, 3]^2)   # the "correct nonlinear terms"

comparison <- t(sapply(c(0, 0.8), function(rho) {
  d <- simulate(rho)
  raw <- cv.glmnet(d$X_tr, d$y_tr, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
  aug <- cv.glmnet(augment(d$X_tr), d$y_tr, alpha = 1, nfolds = 10)
  c(rho              = rho,
    lasso_linear     = mean((d$y_te - predict(raw, d$X_te, s = "lambda.min"))^2),
    lasso_with_terms = mean((d$y_te - predict(aug, augment(d$X_te), s = "lambda.min"))^2),
    noise_floor      = 0.1^2)
}))
round(comparison, 4)
     rho lasso_linear lasso_with_terms noise_floor
[1,] 0.0       0.2434           0.0100        0.01
[2,] 0.8       0.2487           0.0097        0.01

The simulation settles the second half of the claim. Supplying sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2 as two extra columns drops lasso’s test MSE from about 0.2430.243 to 0.01000.0100 with independent covariates, and from about 0.2490.249 to 0.00970.0097 with correlation 0.80.8. Both land at the irreducible noise variance σ2=0.01\sigma^2=0.01. The response is linear in those features, so the structural disadvantage disappears completely instead of remaining.

The conclusion stallur10 draws is still right, and worth keeping: one dataset per setting cannot establish that correlation always helps KNN or that either method is generally better. Only the explanation of the nonlinearity needs correcting. It is also worth noting that the assignment forbids adding nonlinear terms to the lasso model, so the point is about why the comparison is structured the way it is, not about a fit the author should have run.

My GitHub Issue. I posted this review as stallur10/stat432-fall2026 issue #2.
